What Is Excessive Agency in AI?

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 17 November 2026 · 5-minute read · Distribution

In short: Excessive agency is the risk that an AI system holds more tools, permissions or freedom to act than its task needs, so that a hallucination or a manipulated input turns into a damaging action. OWASP lists it as LLM06 in its 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications. It is the reason prompt injection becomes a breach rather than a bad answer, and it is fixed by scoping, not by smarter models.

Key points

  • OWASP defines excessive agency as the vulnerability that enables damaging actions when a model produces unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated output.
  • It has three root causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy.
  • OWASP's December 2025 Top 10 for Agentic Applications adds a principle of "least agency": the minimum autonomy needed for a safe, bounded task.
  • Logging and rate limits reduce the damage but do not prevent it; scoping and approval do.
  • For commercial agents, the most common excess is a send or delete capability on a tool that only needed to read.

What excessive agency means

OWASP describes excessive agency as "the vulnerability that enables damaging actions to be performed" in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated model output. The trigger can be anything: a hallucination, a direct or indirect prompt injection, or a compromised plug-in or peer agent. The point is that the model will sometimes be wrong, and agency decides what being wrong costs.

OWASP breaks it into three root causes.

Root causeWhat it looks likeOWASP example
Excessive functionalityThe agent has tools it does not needA document reader whose extension can also modify and delete
Excessive permissionsA tool has broader access than its taskA read-only lookup connected with an account that can update and delete
Excessive autonomyHigh-impact actions run without verificationA deletion feature that runs without asking the user

Why it matters for a commercial team

OWASP's own attack scenario is a commercial one. An assistant reads a user's email in order to summarise it, but the mail plug-in it uses can also send. An attacker emails hidden instructions; the model searches the inbox for sensitive information and forwards it. OWASP's three fixes are a read-only extension, a read-only OAuth scope, and requiring the user to review and send every draft.

The same pattern is easy to reproduce in sales and account work. A CRM connector installed by an admin can inherit that admin's rights. An email integration approved for reading may also be able to send. A shared service account can let one agent see every user's files, which is OWASP's own example of excessive permissions. None of this is visible from the agent's interface, which is why OWASP treats it as a design flaw rather than a model flaw.

The agentic list published in December 2025 extends the concern. It includes ASI02, tool misuse and exploitation, and ASI03, identity and privilege abuse, where agents reuse or escalate inherited credentials. Its guiding principle is "least agency": granting agents only the minimum autonomy required to perform safe, bounded tasks. The NCSC adds a related rule: an LLM's privileges should drop to those of the party whose information it is processing.

Agency is set by what the agent can touch, not by what it is asked to do.

How to scope an agent

lowob treats autonomy as a dial with five settings: 0 answer, 1 draft, 2 act with approval, 3 act and report, 4 act alone. Excessive agency is any gap between where the dial sits on paper and what the agent's tools and credentials actually allow. OWASP's eight mitigations map onto a short review.

CheckPass condition
Tool inventoryEvery tool is needed for the current task; unused or abandoned ones are removed
Narrow toolsPurpose-built functions rather than open shell, URL-fetch or "do anything" tools
PermissionsDownstream systems grant the least access, enforced by those systems
User contextThe agent acts as a specific user with narrow scopes, not a shared admin account
ApprovalA person approves high-impact actions such as sending, paying or deleting
Complete mediationAuthorisation is checked in the downstream system, not left to the model
MonitoringTool calls are logged and rate-limited, to contain damage if the rest fails

A practical test is to read the agent's job description aloud and then list what its credentials allow. If the job is "summarise inbound requests" and the credentials allow sending, editing contacts and exporting the CRM, the difference is the exposure. Close it before raising the dial.

lowob takeaways

  • Assume the model will err. Agency decides whether an error is a bad answer or a bad action.
  • Check three things. Functions, permissions and autonomy, each against the task as written.
  • Enforce outside the model. Permissions belong in the systems the agent calls, not in its prompt.
  • Raise the dial on evidence. Grant more agency task by task, after a record of low errors.

Common questions

What is excessive agency in OWASP's Top 10 for LLMs?

It is risk LLM06 in the 2025 list: an AI system given more functionality, permissions or autonomy than it needs, so faulty or manipulated output leads to harmful actions.

What is the difference between excessive agency and prompt injection?

Prompt injection is one way a model is manipulated. Excessive agency is what lets that manipulation do damage. An injected agent with read-only tools can do far less harm.

What is the principle of least agency?

A principle in OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications: give agents only the minimum autonomy needed to perform safe, bounded tasks.

How do you prevent excessive agency in AI agents?

Remove unneeded tools, narrow each tool's functions, grant least-privilege access in downstream systems, act in the user's context and require human approval for high-impact actions.

Sources and notes

  • OWASP Gen AI Security Project, LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency, 2025. Community standard; the source of the root causes, mitigations and email scenario above.
  • TechRepublic, OWASP drops first AI agent risk list, 19 December 2025. Press summary of the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, including the least-agency principle.
  • UK National Cyber Security Centre, Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse), 8 December 2025. Government guidance on reducing LLM privileges and relying on deterministic safeguards.
  • The autonomy dial and scoping review are lowob's working method.
